# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.” 
 You can find the discussion draft text here . 
 You can find the section-by-section summary of the discussion draft here . 
 You can read Congressman Obernolte’s and Congresswoman Trahan’s op-ed here .

US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act - DLA Piper GENIE 

 United States 

 US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act

 8 June 2026 
 6 min read 
 By Tony Samp , Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr , Michael Atleson and Alicia Smith 

 LinkedIn 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 Saved to bookmarks . 

 Related topics

 At a glance

 Bipartisan lawmakers have released a 269-page discussion draft of the ‘Great American AI Act’, aiming to establish a comprehensive federal AI framework.

 The draft focuses on national uniformity, workforce impacts, and US leadership, including proposed federal pre-emption of certain state AI laws.

 It introduces transparency and oversight requirements for frontier AI developers, including reporting obligations and mandatory third-party audits.

 The bill includes whistleblower protections and potential civil penalties for non-compliance with key obligations.

 Stakeholder feedback is being sought before formal introduction, although early opposition has already emerged from some groups.

 On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence ( AI ) legislation titled the 'Great American AI Act' ( GAAIA ). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in  supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the  House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition  hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills

 All three sections borrow heavily from  recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable pre-emption provisions

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. ' The bill explains that the purpose of pre-emption is to allow the federal government to 'establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks .' Pre-emption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or pre-empt state laws or rules of 'general applicability.' Therefore, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating  companion bots  and  commercial chatbot interactions .

Breaking Down the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - AAF 

 Insight
 July 21, 2026
 Breaking Down the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act
 Angela Luna
 Executive Summary 

 The Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft represents Congress’ most significant attempt to establish a federal governance framework for frontier artificial intelligence (AI) development—the most advanced, powerful, general-purpose AI models available—while largely preserving state authority over AI deployment and consumer applications.

 Amid a growing patchwork of state AI laws, the bill seeks to establish a single federal baseline—rooted in transparency and accountability standards—for the development of frontier AI, with proponents arguing that nationally consistent standards can better support innovation while reducing regulatory fragmentation.

 While the bill seeks to offer a middle ground between highly prescriptive and lighter-touch approaches and addresses several important aspects of the AI policy debate, it also raises important questions about where to draw the line between AI development and deployment, whether transparency and accountability are sufficient to govern frontier AI risks, and whether state preemption leaves enough room to address other AI regulatory issues.

 Introduction 

 The recently released Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft represents Congress’ most significant attempt to establish a federal governance framework for frontier artificial intelligence (AI) development—the most powerful and general-purpose AI models available—while largely preserving state authority over AI deployment and consumer applications. By releasing the bill as a discussion draft, the sponsors seek feedback from industry, academia, civil society, and the public before formally introducing the legislation.

 Amid a growing patchwork of state AI laws, the bill seeks to establish a single federal baseline—rooted in transparency and accountability standards—for the development of frontier AI. Proponents argue that nationally consistent standards will reduce regulatory fragmentation and better support innovation.

 While the bill seeks to offer a middle ground between highly prescriptive and lighter-touch approaches and addresses several important aspects of the AI policy debate, it also raises important questions about where to draw the line between AI development and deployment, whether transparency and accountability are sufficient to govern frontier AI risks, and whether state preemption leaves enough room to address other regulatory issues in AI.

 Background 

 The release of the GAAIA discussion draft comes at a critical moment in the U.S. AI policy debate. As AI capabilities advance, policymakers have shifted between “ precautionary principle ” and “ permissionless innovation ” paradigms for governing AI. For example, the Biden Administration emphasized AI safety while the Trump Administration has focused on innovation and infrastructure expansion. Although the two administrations adopted different policy priorities, both primarily relied on executive orders, some voluntary guidelines, and agency guidance that can shift with each election cycle. Congress, meanwhile, has not passed any comprehensive legislation governing AI development, while states have been leading on preventing algorithmic discrimination, banning deepfakes, and enforcing safety requirements for AI systems.

 While federal policies provided flexibility during the early years of generative AI—where the primary concerns were chatbot hallucinations or students using AI to complete assignments—they are proving insufficient as frontier AI systems raise broader questions related to cybersecurity, national security, health care, finance, and other critical sectors. The recent controversy surrounding Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable 5 models illustrates this challenge. Amid growing cybersecurity concerns from Anthropic models, the White House instituted ad hoc restrictions based on existing export control law, ordering the company to suspend access to any foreign users, which prompted Anthropic to completely ban the models from all its users to avoid noncompliance risks. This case highlights how, in the absence of a clear statutory framework, governments and developers alike may face uncertainty over how advanced AI systems should be managed. In this context, GAAIA represents one of Congress’ most ambitious attempts to establish an AI federal regulatory framework for those AI systems. Before formal introduction of the bill, its sponsors, Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), released GAAIA as a discussion draft to invite feedback from industry, academia, civil society, and the public.

 The Great American AI Act 

 At four titles and 269 pages, the GAAIA discussion draft covers a wide range of AI policy issues. Its core provisions focus on frontier AI governance, cybersecurity, and federal preemption, while other sections address workforce development, free speech, and international cooperation.

 Frontier AI and Cybersecurity Governance 

 These provisions are the heart of the discussion draft, focusing on the risks arising from development of frontier AI systems and how to mitigate them, particularly those with implications for national security, cybersecurity, and catastrophic risk.

 The draft bill would provide statutory authorization and funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). CAISI, a division of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, was first established as the U.S. AI Safety Institute by an executive order under the Biden Administration in 2023. Notably, CAISI would serve as the federal government’s technical authority on frontier AI, developing voluntary standards while evaluating the capabilities, risks, and evolution of frontier AI systems developed domestically and abroad.

 The draft bill would also establish a frontier AI transparency and independent verification regime. Rather than requiring government approval before deployment, the bill requires companies to publicly disclose how they identify, evaluate, and mitigate catastrophic risks associated with their models. Developers must publish a frontier AI safety framework, report on their testing and risk mitigation practices, and notify regulators when serious safety incidents occur. Additionally, licensed third-party auditors, known as Independent Verification Organizations, would be responsible for reviewing whether companies are complying with their own safety frameworks and whether their risk mitigation measures are adequate.

 Finally, the draft bill’s cybersecurity provisions focus on strengthening the infrastructure and software systems that support frontier AI models. It would reauthorize the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035, allowing companies to share cyber threat information without raising antitrust concerns.  An expansive bipartisan House draft bill issued Thursday would set up a federal framework for artificial intelligence governance, laying groundwork for the codification of a key federal AI standards center and calling for accountability in government AI adoption.

 The discussion draft, led by Reps. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., and Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., came two days after the White House issued an artificial intelligence-focused executive order asking for early access to AI models for oversight. The draft is “intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced,” the lawmakers said in a release.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day,” Trahan said in a statement . “This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation.”

 The draft bill would formally codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in the Commerce Department, with $100 million per year authorized for fiscal 2027-2029. The center would develop voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, as well as evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress. 

 Advertisement 

 Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last June rebranded the U.S. AI Safety Institute , launched during the Biden administration, as the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. Despite being established by the executive branch in late 2024, the organization lacks a formal authorization from Congress.

 Deemed the “Great American AI Act,” the bill would also require the Government Accountability Office to evaluate federal AI adoption progress, identify federal statutes and regulations that “directly affect AI innovation or unduly burden AI infrastructure (including energy)” and provide legislative and administrative recommendations, according to a bill summary.

 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology,” Obernolte said.

 The bill draft, nearing 270 pages, would also add penalties for using AI to impersonate government officials, require large frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the government and direct the Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics to revise federal surveys to incorporate AI use and adoption questions. 

 A key issue in American AI governance over the last year, the draft also includes provisions that would preempt states from issuing their own laws regulating the development of frontier AI models — though it would allow for states to pass laws of “general applicability” related to AI and regulate models after they’ve been deployed.

 Advertisement 

 The bill would also require the Energy Department, the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the National Science Foundation to establish a testbed program for public and private sector labs and entities to collaborate on evaluating AI systems.

 The Energy Department and NIST would additionally jointly lead the nation’s international AI standards development to “form coalitions with like-minded governments to promote private sector-led standards adoption, advocate for U.S.-developed AI standards internationally, counter foreign adversary influence, facilitate cross-border AI R&D collaboration, and share cybersecurity best practices,” a draft summary said, expressly excluding China.

 “America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” co-sponsor Rep. Erin Houchin, R-Ind., said in the statement. “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections.”

 The draft bill would authorize the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to award grants to maintainers of widely used open-source software for security improvements, including those for patching, maintenance and security audits. The GAO would evaluate security protocols protecting AI model weights and the security of the open-source software ecosystem.

 NIST and NSF would establish several grants and prizes, including one to broaden participation in AI research, education and workforce development. The National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, also a product of the Biden administration and housed in NSF, would be formally codified by the legislation to procure and provide data, training and resources for AI development for the public and private sectors.

 Advertisement 

 A discussion draft is a bill that has not yet been formally introduced for congressional action. The sponsors did not indicate when or if the bill would be introduced, but did encourage all to send feedback to GAAIA@mail.house.gov. 

 “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right,” Trahan said.

{"path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md", "content": "# ACIA comment letter - Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

**DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF - NOT FOR TRANSMISSION**
Brackets contain placeholders or items to confirm before transmission. See `00_cover_note.md` for sourcing and assumptions.

---

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
[Street address]
Washington, DC [ZIP]

[October ___, 2026]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Submitted by email to GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, released June 4 with Reps. Scott Franklin, Suhas Subramanyam, Erin Houchin and Scott Peters. A 269-page bipartisan draft, published for comment before introduction, is a service to the process and we thank you for it. Our comments also address the frontier-governance provisions your offices introduced July 23 as the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925). They apply with equal force to that bill.

ACIA is a Washington-based coalition of about 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips and facilities that will determine whether the United States leads this technology.

Our position in brief. ACIA supports Section 121's preemption of state laws regulating AI model development, and we ask that you make it permanent. We ask you to strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111(f) and 111(g), the federally licensed audit regime in Section 112, and the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in Section 102, together with its $100 million annual authorization and its fee authority. We support several other provisions and list them below.

## 1. One national standard: support Section 121, and make it permanent

The state patchwork is no longer a projection. California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect Jan. 1 and requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the Governor's Office of Emergency Services within 15 days, or within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by the chapter amendment signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027, and requires reporting within 72 hours to a new office inside the Department of Financial Services. Your own FAQ notes a third state frontier-model statute, Illinois' SB 315. Three states, three definitions, three regulators, one industry.

The costs are not hypothetical. In August, ACIA surveyed its members (86 respondents; not a probability sample). Sixty-one percent cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue. Among members subject to both California and New York obligations, the median compliance burden was 6.5 full-time employees. Thirty-four percent of our startup members reported delaying a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

Section 121 answers this. It preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate AI model development, and it expressly leaves untouched laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state regulation of AI use and deployment. That is the right line. As your FAQ notes, it also reaches development-side mandates beyond frontier safety, including California's AB 2013 training-data disclosure requirements. ACIA supports Section 121 without reservation.

Our request is simple: strike the three-year sunset. A national standard with an expiry date is not a standard; it is a timer. Compliance programs, product roadmaps and financing decisions are built on horizons of five to 10 years, and relief that lapses in 2029 does not change them. The draft already sunsets Sections 111 and 112 on the same three-year clock, which would put the entire framework back before Congress in the same year. If the Committee wants a checkpoint, put it on the studies and reports, not on the preemption.

## 2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate (Section 101(7), 111(f), 111(g))

Sections 111(f) and 111(g) require a frontier developer, defined as an entity that has trained a model above the draft's 10^26 computing-operation threshold and had more than $50 million in gross revenue the prior calendar year, to report a critical safety incident to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. State attorneys general may opt in to receive the reports. Violations of Sections 111 and 112 carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per day per violation.

The problem is what must be reported. Section 101(7) defines a critical safety incident as (A) unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights; (B) a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; or (C) loss of control of such model.

Subparagraph (A) describes a real, concrete risk, and we address it below. Subparagraphs (B) and (C) describe speculative doomsday scenarios for which there is no record. No frontier model has caused mass casualties. No frontier model has acted outside human control. The draft's own definition of catastrophic risk in Section 101(6), involving more than 50 deaths or more than $1 billion in damage, describes an event that no AI system in commercial use has approached.

The evidence behind these scenarios comes from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations. The most publicized recent example is Anthropic's June 2025 study, "Agentic Misalignment," which placed 16 leading models in hypothetical corporate environments, assigned them harmless business goals, and tested whether they would act against the companies running them. Some models, in some scenarios, chose blackmail. The researchers themselves framed the tests as binary choices, and observers noted that a real-world setting would offer many other options. Those demonstrations tell us how a model behaves when a researcher designs a scenario with two doors. They tell us nothing about the world.

These claims have been amplified in Washington by a small, well-funded advocacy network. Open Philanthropy, renamed Coefficient Giving in November 2025, reports having directed more than $4 billion in giving since 2014 and is a leading funder of the organizations pressing the catastrophic-risk case; the first AI-safety groups backed by technology billionaires registered federal lobbyists in late 2023. ACIA does not question anyone's motives. We question whether Congress should write this network's risk assessment into the United States Code.

The compliance cost is real. Our members estimate a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function (IQR $140,000 to $720,000). That buys no safety. It buys the systems, counsel and personnel needed to decide, on a 24-hour clock, whether an internal control failure is a federal reporting event.

It also centralizes risk. Mandatory reports describing security-relevant events would sit in a federal repository available, by opt-in, to state attorneys general. Aggregating sensitive security information in one place is itself a security decision, and the draft makes it lightly.

Requested change: strike Sections 111(f) and 111(g), and strike subparagraphs (B) and (C) of Section 101(7). If the Committee retains a reporting obligation of any kind, it should be confined to verified unauthorized access to model weights and routed through existing federal cyber channels, with no state attorney general opt-in.

## 3. Strike the CAISI codification and its funding (Section 102, and Section 112 with it)

Section 102 writes CAISI into statute at the Department of Commerce with a Director appointed by the Secretary, authority to develop voluntary AI security guidelines, authority to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, support for synthetic content detection tools, and administration of the licensing regime for independent verification organizations. It authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 to carry out Sections 102, 111 and 112, funds that remain available until expended. It adds authority to collect fees from licensed auditors and from large frontier developers.

Read that list again. A body that licenses auditors, receives mandatory incident reports, monitors an industry's progress and collects fees from the companies it oversees is not a standards body. It is a regulator with an appropriations line, and its budget grows with the compliance burden it administers. That is regulatory capture of a new agency on the day it is born.

CAISI already exists administratively. Commerce created it in June 2025 by renaming the U.S. AI Safety Institute. Codifying it now, with new authorities attached, converts an industry-facing standards shop into the enforcement spine of Sections 111 and 112. Section 112 cannot survive on its own: its auditors are licensed by the CAISI Director and its regime is funded through Section 102. Striking CAISI requires striking Section 112.

The mandatory audit mandate is not a state consensus. New York dropped the RAISE Act's third-party audit requirement in the March chapter amendment, and California's law never included one. The draft would federalize a mandate that the two leading states considered and declined.

NIST's mission is nonregulatory measurement science. Done well, that mission is genuinely valuable to our members, and ACIA supports funding it. Our members need better benchmarks, better evaluation methods and better metrology, not a federal clearinghouse for speculative incident reports. ACIA will ask appropriators to defund CAISI and to return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

Requested change: strike Section 102, including the authorization of appropriations in Section 102(e) and the fee authority in Section 102(f), and strike Section 112. Preserve genuinely useful measurement work as voluntary NIST activity under existing authorities.

## 4. Provisions ACIA supports

The draft does much that we support, and the Committee should hear that clearly.

Section 301 reauthorizes the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035, keeping a proven threat-sharing regime alive. Section 311 authorizes CISA grants to maintainers of widely used open-source software, addressing a real infrastructure risk.

Section 321 requires a Government Accountability Office review of model-weight, data center and open-source security. That is the risk that matters. In June, a Commerce directive grounded a leading American frontier model for two and a half weeks over concerns about foreign access; the order was lifted June 30. Whatever one thinks of that episode, it showed that unauthorized access and foreign diversion of advanced model weights are the concrete frontier security questions of the day, and that ad hoc use of existing authorities carries real costs for American companies. We would rather the Committee build on Section 321 than on Section 111.

We also support Section 122's GAO review of federal impediments to AI innovation, including burdens on energy and infrastructure; Section 123's NIST pilot on model documentation, which we would keep voluntary; Sections 131 and 132's increased penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for impersonation of federal officials; and Section 141's study of government pressure on AI platforms.

Title IV is welcome. Section 401's testbed program, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, and Section 411's direction to lead international standards work through coalitions of like-minded governments while countering foreign adversary influence all serve American leadership. On Section 113, the whistleblower protections, we take no position at this stage and will submit technical comments.

## 5. Requested changes, in order

1. Section 121: strike the three-year sunset and make preemption permanent.
2. Section 101(7): strike subparagraphs (B) and (C).
3. Sections 111(f) and 111(g): strike the incident-reporting mandate.
4. Sections 111(a) through 111(e): strike the mandatory federal frontier AI framework and transparency-report regime, or convert them to voluntary practice. Our members already publish frontier safety frameworks. A federal mandate reproduces at the national level the state obligations Section 121 removes.
5. Section 112: strike the federally licensed audit regime.
6. Section 102: strike the codification, the $100 million annual authorization and the fee authority.
7. In appropriations, fund NIST's core measurement-science mission rather than CAISI.
8. Support Sections 122, 123, 131, 132, 141, 301, 311, 321, 401 and 411, and the codification of NAIRR.

## Conclusion

Your draft is a genuine attempt at a bipartisan national framework, and the preemption at its center is the most important thing in it. ACIA's members will build under one national standard or under a patchwork. Those are the choices. We ask the Committee to keep the preemption, make it permanent, and decline to build the federal reporting and audit regime that would ride along with it.

ACIA would welcome the chance to work with Committee staff on these sections. Please contact [Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy], at [email] or [phone].

Respectfully,

**Grant Holloway**
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

[Attachment available on request: ACIA member compliance-cost survey, August 2026, aggregate results.]

Q1 (Majority E&C): If you support preemption, why not incident reporting? It's lighter than SB 53.
A: Preemption is about jurisdiction: one national standard instead of a patchwork. It does not follow that Congress should add a federal reporting mandate. Section 101(7) requires developers to report "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" to CAISI on a 15-day clock, 24 hours if "imminent," with penalties up to $1 million a day. No frontier model has caused mass casualties or escaped human control; the underlying scenarios are contrived lab demonstrations. Supporting preemption doesn't mean supporting every federal obligation attached to it. Our members prefer relief to relocation: strike the mandate and let preemption do its work. (~100 words) Good.

Q2 (Trahan-aligned): What federal safety obligations would you accept?
A: Ones tied to verifiable risks, with defined costs. We support Section 301's extension of cyber threat sharing, Section 311's open-source security grants, Section 321's GAO review of model-weight security, Sections 131-132's fraud and impersonation penalties, and Section 122's GAO review. Our members already publish frontier safety frameworks and run internal red-teaming; we'd accept a voluntary NIST measurement and evaluation role, and reporting confined to verified unauthorized access to model weights through existing federal cyber channels. What we cannot accept is codifying "catastrophic risk" and "loss of control" as legal categories. Those definitions have no evidentiary record, and they would outlast this Congress. (~110 words)

Q3 (Senate Commerce): Three years or permanent?
A: Permanent. A standard with an expiry date is a timer, not a standard. Compliance programs, roadmaps and financing decisions run five to 10 years; relief that lapses in 2029 does not change them. The draft already sunsets Sections 111 and 112 on the same three-year clock, so Congress would relitigate the whole framework in one year. And the sunset guarantees the patchwork returns: SB 53 is in effect now and the RAISE Act takes effect January 1. If Congress wants a checkpoint, put it on the studies and reports, not on the preemption. (~95 words)

**DRAFT - for internal use with E&C member offices | October 2026**

## Keep the preemption. Drop the federal AI regulator.

Reps. Obernolte and Trahan's discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (269 pages, released June 4) is the first serious bipartisan federal AI framework. Its center is right: Section 121 preempts state laws that specifically regulate AI model development, while leaving alone state laws on AI use, deployment and general applicability.

But the draft builds a new federal regulator beside that standard. Section 111 mandates reporting of "critical safety incidents" to a codified Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). Section 102 funds CAISI at $100 million a year and gives it fee authority. Section 112 forces developers into federally licensed, semi-annual third-party audits.

**Why it matters**

- The patchwork is here. California's SB 53 is in effect; New York's RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Illinois has enacted a third frontier-model law.
- ACIA's August member survey (86 respondents, not a probability sample): 61% cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue. Members subject to both California and New York spend a median 6.5 FTEs on compliance. 34% of startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past year.
- The reporting mandate is keyed to unfounded scenarios. Section 101(7) requires developers to report "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control." No frontier model has caused mass casualties or escaped human control. The evidence base is thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations.
- Members estimate a median $310,000 one-time cost just to stand up an incident-reporting function. It buys no safety.

2. **Strike incident reporting.** Remove Section 111(f) and 111(g) and the "risk-mitigation failure" and "loss of control" triggers in Section 101(7).
3. **Strike the audit mandate.** Remove Section 112's federally licensed IVO regime.
4. **Strike CAISI.** Remove Section 102's codification, $100 million annual authorization and fee authority. Fund NIST's core measurement-science mission instead.
5. **Keep the concrete-risk provisions.** Support Sections 122, 123, 131, 132, 141, 301, 311, 321, 401 and 411, and NAIRR codification.

**Bottom line:** Build one national standard and fund measurement science. Do not write speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code.

{"content": "# ACIA staff Q&A: anticipated Hill questions on the GAAIA comments

**DRAFT - for internal prep | October 2026.** Sources: the four questions logged from September Hill meetings. Answers are 120 words or fewer. Positions per Messaging Guide v4.

---

## 1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not support incident reporting? It's lighter than SB 53."

Preemption is about jurisdiction, one national standard instead of a patchwork. It does not follow that Congress should add a federal reporting mandate on top. Section 101(7) makes a "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" or a "loss of control" a reportable federal incident, on a 15-day clock, 24 hours for anything deemed imminent, with penalties up to $1 million a day. No frontier model has caused mass casualties or escaped human control. The underlying scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. Supporting preemption does not mean supporting every federal obligation drafted alongside it. Our members want relief, not relocation of the same mandates to Washington.

## 2. Minority staff: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"

Obligations tied to verifiable risks and defined costs. We support Section 301's extension of cyber threat information sharing, Section 311's grants for critical open-source maintainers, Section 321's GAO review of model-weight and data center security, Sections 131 and 132's penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials, and Section 122's review of federal impediments to innovation. Our members already publish frontier safety frameworks and run red-teaming. We would accept a voluntary NIST measurement and evaluation role, and reporting confined to verified unauthorized access to model weights through existing federal cyber channels. What we cannot accept is codifying "catastrophic risk" and "loss of control" as legal categories. Those definitions have no evidentiary record and would outlast this Congress.

## 3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"

Permanent. A national standard with an expiry date is a timer, not a standard. Compliance programs, product roadmaps and financing decisions run five to 10 years, so relief that lapses in 2029 does not change them. The draft already sunsets Sections 111 and 112 on the same three-year clock, which would put the entire framework back before Congress in a single year. And the sunset guarantees the patchwork returns: California's law is in effect now and New York's takes effect Jan. 1. If members want a checkpoint, attach it to the studies and reports, not to the preemption itself. Permanence is also what the White House framework called for in March.

## 4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"

The level is not the problem; the mission is. Section 102 does not fund measurement science. It funds a body that licenses its own auditors, receives mandatory incident reports, monitors industry progress and collects fees from the developers it oversees, $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 plus fee authority, with funds available until expended. That is a regulator with an appropriations line. CAISI already exists administratively; Commerce created it in June 2025 by renaming the AI Safety Institute. Our request is straightforward: do not codify it, and do not fund it. Appropriate to NIST's core measurement-science mission instead. That work is genuinely valuable to our members.

---

**Prep note for the team:** If pressed on the Anthropic "Agentic Misalignment" study, the response is that the researchers built binary, hypothetical corporate scenarios and noted the artificial framing themselves. Do not describe the behavior as implausible or as a live risk; say the study shows how a model behaves in a setup with two doors, not in the world.

# ACIA comment letter - Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

**DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF - NOT FOR TRANSMISSION**
Brackets contain placeholders or items to confirm before transmission. See `00_cover_note.md` for sourcing and assumptions.

---

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
[Street address]
Washington, DC [ZIP]

[October ___, 2026]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Submitted by email to GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, released June 4 with Reps. Scott Franklin, Suhas Subramanyam, Erin Houchin and Scott Peters. A 269-page bipartisan draft, published for comment before introduction, is a service to the process and we thank you for it. Our comments also address the frontier-governance provisions your offices introduced July 23 as the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925). They apply with equal force to that bill.

ACIA is a Washington-based coalition of about 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips and facilities that will determine whether the United States leads this technology.

Our position in brief. ACIA supports Section 121's preemption of state laws regulating AI model development, and we ask that you make it permanent. We ask you to strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111(f) and 111(g), the federally licensed audit regime in Section 112, and the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in Section 102, together with its $100 million annual authorization and its fee authority. We support several other provisions and list them below.

## 1. One national standard: support Section 121, and make it permanent

The state patchwork is no longer a projection. California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect Jan. 1 and requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the Governor's Office of Emergency Services within 15 days, or within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by the chapter amendment signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027, and requires reporting within 72 hours to a new office inside the Department of Financial Services. Your own FAQ notes a third state frontier-model statute, Illinois' SB 315. Three states, three definitions, three regulators, one industry.

The costs are not hypothetical. In August, ACIA surveyed its members (86 respondents; not a probability sample). Sixty-one percent cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue. Members complying with both SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel report a median 6.5 full-time employees of compliance effort. Thirty-four percent of our startup members delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Members that publish a frontier safety framework spend a median $1.4 million a year maintaining it.

Section 121 answers this. It preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate AI model development, and it expressly leaves untouched laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state regulation of AI use and deployment. That is the right line. As your FAQ notes, it also reaches development-side mandates beyond frontier safety, including California's AB 2013 training-data disclosure requirements. ACIA supports Section 121 without reservation.

Our request is simple: strike the three-year sunset. A national standard with an expiry date is not a standard; it is a timer. Compliance programs, product roadmaps and financing decisions are built on horizons of five to 10 years, and relief that lapses in 2029 does not change them. The draft already sunsets Sections 111 and 112 on the same three-year clock, which would put the entire framework back before Congress in the same year. If the Committee wants a checkpoint, put it on the studies and reports, not on the preemption.

## 2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate (Section 101(7), 111(f), 111(g))

Sections 111(f) and 111(g) require a frontier developer, defined as an entity that has trained or initiated the training of a model above the draft's 10^26 computing-operation threshold and had more than $50 million in gross revenue, counting affiliates, in the prior calendar year, to report a critical safety incident to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. State attorneys general may opt in to receive the reports. Violations of Sections 111 and 112 carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per day per violation.

The problem is what must be reported. Section 101(7) defines a critical safety incident as (A) unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights; (B) a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; or (C) loss of control of such model.

Subparagraph (A) describes a real, concrete risk, and we address it below. Subparagraphs (B) and (C) describe speculative doomsday scenarios for which there is no record. There is no documented case of a frontier model causing mass casualties or acting outside human control. The draft's own definition of catastrophic risk in Section 101(6), involving more than 50 deaths or more than $1 billion in damage, describes an event that no AI system in commercial use has approached.

The evidence behind these scenarios comes from thought experiments and contrived labora
... [2019 chars truncated] ...
ts and routed through existing federal cyber channels, with no state attorney general opt-in.

## 3. Strike the CAISI codification and its funding (Section 102, and Section 112 with it)

Section 102 writes CAISI into statute at the Department of Commerce with a Director appointed by the Secretary, authority to develop voluntary AI security guidelines, authority to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, support for synthetic content detection tools, and administration of the licensing regime for independent verification organizations. It authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 to carry out Sections 102, 111 and 112, funds that remain available until expended. It adds authority to collect fees from licensed auditors and from large frontier developers.

Read that list again. A body that licenses auditors, receives mandatory incident reports, monitors an industry's progress and collects fees from the companies it oversees is not a standards body. It is a regulator with an appropriations line, and its budget grows with the compliance burden it administers. That is regulatory capture of a new agency on the day it is born.

CAISI already exists administratively. Commerce created it in June 2025 by renaming the U.S. AI Safety Institute. Codifying it now, with new authorities attached, converts an industry-facing standards shop into the enforcement spine of Sections 111 and 112. Section 112 cannot survive on its own: its auditors are licensed by the CAISI Director and its regime is funded through Section 102. Striking CAISI requires striking Section 112.

The mandatory audit mandate is not a state consensus. New York dropped the RAISE Act's third-party audit requirement in the March chapter amendment, and California's law never included one. The draft would federalize a mandate that the two leading states considered and declined.

NIST's mission is nonregulatory measurement science. Done well, that mission is genuinely valuable to our members, and ACIA supports funding it. Our members need better benchmarks, better evaluation methods and better metrology, not a federal clearinghouse for speculative incident reports. ACIA will ask appropriators to defund CAISI and to return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

Requested change: strike Section 102, including the authorization of appropriations in Section 102(e) and the fee authority in Section 102(f), and strike Section 112. Preserve genuinely useful measurement work as voluntary NIST activity under existing authorities.

## 4. Provisions ACIA supports

The draft does much that we support, and the Committee should hear that clearly.

Section 301 reauthorizes the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035, keeping a proven threat-sharing regime alive. Section 311 authorizes CISA grants to maintainers of widely used open-source software, addressing a real infrastructure risk.

Section 321 requires a Government Accountability Office review of model-weight, data center and open-source security. That is the risk that matters. In June, a Commerce directive grounded a leading American frontier model for two and a half weeks over concerns about foreign access; the order was lifted June 30. Whatever one thinks of that episode, it showed that unauthorized access and foreign diversion of advanced model weights are the concrete frontier security questions of the day, and that ad hoc use of existing authorities carries real costs for American companies. We would rather the Committee build on Section 321 than on Section 111.

We also support Section 122's GAO review of federal impediments to AI innovation, including burdens on energy and infrastructure; Section 123's NIST pilot on model documentation, which we would keep voluntary; Sections 131 and 132's increased penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for impersonation of federal officials; and Section 141's study of government pressure on AI platforms.

Title IV is welcome. Section 401's testbed program, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, and Section 411's direction to lead international standards work through coalitions of like-minded governments while countering foreign adversary influence all serve American leadership. On Section 113, the whistleblower protections, we take no position at this stage and will submit technical comments.

## 5. Requested changes, in order

1. Section 121: strike the three-year sunset and make preemption permanent.
2. Section 101(7): strike subparagraphs (B) and (C).
3. Sections 111(f) and 111(g): strike the incident-reporting mandate.
4. Sections 111(a) through 111(e): strike the mandatory federal frontier AI framework and transparency-report regime, or convert them to voluntary practice. Our members already publish frontier safety frameworks. A federal mandate reproduces at the national level the state obligations Section 121 removes.
5. Section 112: strike the federally licensed audit regime.
6. Section 102: strike the codification, the $100 million annual authorization and the fee authority.
7. In appropriations, fund NIST's core measurement-science mission rather than CAISI.
8. Support Sections 122, 123, 131, 132, 141, 301, 311, 321, 401 and 411, and the codification of NAIRR.

## Conclusion

Your draft is a genuine attempt at a bipartisan national framework, and the preemption at its center is the most important thing in it. ACIA's members will build under one national standard or under a patchwork. Those are the choices. We ask the Committee to keep the preemption, make it permanent, and decline to build the federal reporting and audit regime that would ride along with it.

ACIA would welcome the chance to work with Committee staff on these sections. Please contact [Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy], at [email] or [phone].

Respectfully,

**Grant Holloway**
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

[Attachment available on request: ACIA member compliance-cost survey, August 2026, aggregate results.]

# ACIA one-pager: Great American AI Act discussion draft (House E&C)

**DRAFT - for internal use with E&C member offices | October 2026**

## Keep the preemption. Drop the federal AI regulator.

Reps. Obernolte and Trahan's discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (269 pages, released June 4) is the first serious bipartisan federal AI framework. Its center is right: Section 121 preempts state laws that specifically regulate AI model development, while leaving alone state laws on AI use, deployment and general applicability.

But the draft builds a new federal regulator beside that standard. Section 111 mandates reporting of "critical safety incidents" to a codified Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). Section 102 funds CAISI at $100 million a year and gives it fee authority. Section 112 forces developers into federally licensed, semi-annual third-party audits.

**Why it matters**

- The patchwork is here. California's SB 53 is in effect; New York's RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Illinois has enacted a third frontier-model law.
- ACIA's August member survey (86 respondents, not a probability sample): 61% cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue. Members subject to both California and New York spend a median 6.5 FTEs on compliance. 34% of startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past year.
- The reporting mandate is keyed to unfounded scenarios. Section 101(7) requires developers to report "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control." No frontier model has caused mass casualties or escaped human control. The evidence base is thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations.
- Members estimate a median $310,000 one-time cost just to stand up an incident-reporting function. It buys no safety.
- The mandate exceeds the states. New York dropped third-party audits in March. California never required them.

**ACIA's asks**

1. **Make preemption permanent.** Strike the three-year sunset in Section 121. A national standard with an expiry date is a timer, not a standard.
2. **Strike incident reporting.** Remove Section 111(f) and 111(g) and the "risk-mitigation failure" and "loss of control" triggers in Section 101(7).
3. **Strike the audit mandate.** Remove Section 112's federally licensed IVO regime.
4. **Strike CAISI.** Remove Section 102's codification, $100 million annual authorization and fee authority. Fund NIST's core measurement-science mission instead.
5. **Keep the concrete-risk provisions.** Support Sections 122, 123, 131, 132, 141, 301, 311, 321, 401 and 411, and NAIRR codification.

**Bottom line:** Build one national standard and fund measurement science. Do not write speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code.

Contact: [Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy], ACIA | [email] | [phone]

# GAAIA discussion draft: ACIA asks by section

**DRAFT - for internal use | October 2026.** Section numbers and descriptions checked against the sponsors' discussion draft text, section-by-section summary and staff FAQ (released June 2-4, 2026). Positions per ACIA Messaging Guide v4 (board-approved Sept. 30, 2026).

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 101(6) - "catastrophic risk" definition (50+ deaths or $1B+ damage; CBRN uplift; conduct with no meaningful human oversight) | Oppose codification | Strike with Sections 111-112, which it exists to serve | Writes speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code. |
| Sec. 101(7)(B)-(C) - "critical safety incident" includes failure of risk-mitigation measures and "loss of control" | Oppose | Strike (B) and (C); retain only verified unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights | Reporting should key to events that have happened, not scenarios. |
| Sec. 102 - codifies CAISI at Commerce; voluntary security guidelines; evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress; administer IVO licensing | Oppose | Strike the codification | A standards body that licenses auditors and monitors industry is a regulator, not a standards body. |
| Sec. 102(e) - $100M/yr authorized FY2027-2029 to carry out Secs. 102, 111 and 112 | Oppose | Strike; ask appropriators to fund NIST's core measurement-science mission and defund CAISI | $300 million buys a federal clearinghouse for speculative incident reports. |
| Sec. 102(f) - fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers | Oppose | Strike | Developers should not fund their own regulator. |
| Sec. 111(a)-(e) - mandatory published frontier AI framework (>$500M revenue developers) and per-model transparency reports | Oppose as a federal mandate; support as voluntary practice | Strike or convert to voluntary | Don't federalize the state mandates Sec. 121 preempts; our members already publish frameworks. |
| Sec. 111(f)-(g) - report critical safety incidents to CAISI within 15 days (24 hours if imminent risk); state AG opt-in | Oppose | Strike both subsections; if anything survives, limit to verified model-weight compromise via existing federal cyber channels, no state AG opt-in | Median $310,000 one-time cost to report hypothetical harms to 51 potential enforcers. |
| Sec. 112 - CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations; semi-annual audits; mandatory referral for imminent "catastrophic risk" | Oppose | Strike; keep third-party evaluation voluntary | New York dropped audits in March; California never had them. |
| Sec. 113 - whistleblower protections for employees and contractors | No position | Technical comments only; narrow "AI violation" | No board position; avoid creating a private hook for every arguable claim. |
| Sec. 121 - preemption of state laws specifically regulating AI model development; three-year sunset | Support | Strike the sunset; make preemption permanent | One national standard with an expiry date is a timer, not a standard. |
| Sec. 121 scope - leaves intact state laws on use/deployment, general applicability, common-law remedies | Support | None; confirm coverage of state frontier-development mandates (SB 53, RAISE) and AB 2013 | Our members build once; they cannot build twice for California and New York. |
| Sec. 122 - GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation (incl. energy and infrastructure burdens) | Support | None | Documents federal, not just state, drag on AI infrastructure. |
| Sec. 123 - NIST pilot on AI model documentation templates | Support | Keep the program voluntary | Useful, low-cost, and only works if developers opt in. |
| Sec. 131 - raises max fines from $1M to $2M for AI-enabled mail, wire, bank fraud and money laundering | Support | None | Concrete harms, existing enforcement channels. |
| Sec. 132 - penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials | Support | None | Targets a real and growing abuse. |
| Sec. 141 - Commerce study of government "jawboning" of AI platforms | Support | None | Documents pressure on lawful speech; needs subsequent legislation to bite. |
| Sec. 251 - WARN Act disclosures when AI is a substantial factor in mass layoffs | No position | Technical comments later | Workforce title is outside the board's AI-governance positions. |
| Sec. 301 - reauthorizes Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035 | Support | None | Keeps a proven threat-sharing regime alive. |
| Sec. 311 - CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers; model access for cybersecurity purposes | Support | Confirm liability protection for provided model access | Patches real infrastructure risk without a new mandate. |
| Sec. 321 - GAO report on model-weight, data center and open-source security | Support | None | This is the concrete frontier security risk worth spending on. |
| Sec. 401 - DOE/NIST/NSF AI testbed program with National Labs, NIST and NAIRR | Support | None | Compute access for evaluation, which our members want. |
| Sec. 411 - U.S.-led international standards coalitions with like-minded governments, countering foreign adversary influence | Support | None | American-led standards, not Beijing's. |
| NAIRR codification | Support | None | Broadens access to data and compute for smaller members. |
